title: Constants and Variables in Different Contexts
keywords: constants and variables in different contexts
learning_outcomes: Explain what constants and variables in different contexts contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: superglobals.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Reliable programs represent values deliberately. Variables hold changing values, constants name stable values, and type behavior affects comparisons, conversion, function contracts, and error handling. In this lesson, focus on superglobals; then compare it with environment variables. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use constants and variables in different contexts when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Reliable programs represent values deliberately. Variables hold changing values, constants name stable values, and type behavior affects comparisons, conversion, function contracts, and error handling. For constants and variables in different contexts, begin with superglobals. Also distinguish environment variables; function parameters; class properties. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Constants and Variables in Different Contexts
content_blocks.code:
<?php
final class Tax { public function amount(int $price): int { return intdiv($price, 10); } }
final class Checkout { public function __construct(private Tax $tax) {} public function total(int $price): int { return $price + $this->tax->amount($price); } }
echo (new Checkout(new Tax()))->total(100) . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for constants and variables in different contexts from top to bottom. Start by identifying superglobals, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
